title: How to Keep Growing FOREVER (Unlimited Hypertrophy Method)
summary: A practical masterclass on his 'unlimited hypertrophy method' for delaying and breaking plateaus. It covers evolving rep ranges and evolving sets, why you should not drop weight or swap exercises when you stall, and how to add soft and hard variations in rotation, with limits on how many to use at each training level.
claims: There is no natural limit: with smart progression you can always find a way to improve, so hypertrophy is in theory unlimited
Plateaus cannot be avoided, so accept them; the goal is to hit fewer of them and later, which also protects your love of lifting
Linear schemes like 3x5 and 5x5 raise strength fastest but run you into plateaus soonest; beginners use them because they think strength equals hypertrophy
Evolving rep ranges: with a range like 3x6-10, a PR only needs one more rep; you add weight only once the range is maxed out, with the first set at the ceiling and the others close to it
The rep range sets the weight jump: after 10/9/8 reps at 200 lb on close-grip bench, go to 205 so you still land around 7/6/6 inside the range
With a wider range like 8-15, hitting 15 reps lets you add about 10 lb and still get at least 8
Every working set has to stay in the range, not just the first; if the later sets drop out, the range or the load is wrong
The narrower the range, the more conservative the jumps must be; keep at least four reps between floor and ceiling (6-10, 8-12), because a 5 lb jump means more at higher reps
Evolving sets: if after a weight jump you can't keep all three sets in the range, drop to two sets at the new weight (e.g. 7 and 6 reps), then add the third set back next time
Keep evolving sets between two and four; too many sets on a wide range (e.g. 8 sets of 10-20 squats) means adding weight only every 3-4 months
Evolving ranges give up strength speed for more volume at a useful intensity without the pressure of adding load, which tends to cost technique, form and tempo
Weight jumps on static rep ranges feel like skydiving for advanced lifters; on evolving ranges they are smooth because you've built so much volume at the previous weight
Never take weight off the bar to break a plateau; it only cuts intensity, and if you needed a drop to 70% your earlier programming was a mess
Swapping an exercise when it stalls dodges the plateau instead of breaking it: the fast progress afterwards is neural adaptation to a new skill, not new muscle
For intermediate and advanced lifters, hypertrophy happens exactly when progression gets hard, because that is when the body must build muscle for the extra rep
Log your lifts; many people who keep swapping exercises would find they are at the same numbers they had years ago
Repeating the same weight and reps for two or three sessions is not a plateau but the breaking point where gains happen; longer than that is a real plateau
Grinding into a true plateau with no changes will eventually work but is frustrating and can lead to injury
A variation is a movement on the same line of specificity as another; a rotation alternates two movements in one slot, either on a schedule (week A/B) or by autoregulation for advanced lifters
Only add a variation when a movement keeps stalling despite evolving rep ranges; that shows it needs extra relevant volume from elsewhere
Specificity: an RDL is close to the conventional deadlift and a split squat is far from it; bodybuilders judge specificity by the muscle trained, not by the lift's carryover
A variation must not hurt the main lift; start it at 1-2 sets, about 50% of the main movement's volume, and build up with evolving set ranges
Keep variations few: each one cuts how often you train every lift, so you may lose weight on the bar from forgetting the skill rather than from muscle loss
Use at most five hard variations per movement pattern

Hard variations differ in movement pattern (pull-up vs lat pulldown, squat vs leg press); soft variations are near-identical (high-bar squat vs paused high-bar squat) and you can have as many as you like
Novices should use 0-1 variations per lift, intermediates 1-2 and advanced lifters 3-5
'Optimal' training just means adding complexity once nothing simpler works; novices should keep things minimal for as long as possible
Give a variation a different rep range from the main lift to change intensity and volume, e.g. bench 3x4-8 with close-grip bench 3x6-12, or dips at a lower rep range for more intensity
Soft variations carry over more strength; hard variations hit the muscle differently, may stimulate more growth and help prevent overuse injuries, but each one is a new skill to learn
You should be able to justify every variation and its rep range; never add variations just to cure boredom
If you still plateau with all of this, either recovery is lacking (eat and sleep more), the rep range or weight jumps are wrong, or the plateau is psychological
